clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in TTN, which encodes titin — the giant sarcomeric protein spanning half the sarcomere from Z-disc to M-band that governs passive elasticity and sarcomere assembly.
The clinical spectrum is exceptionally broad and highly domain- and inheritance-dependent, ranging from dominant late-onset distal disease to severe recessive congenital and limb-girdle myopathies.
Tibial muscular dystrophy (Udd myopathy) is a dominant, adult-onset distal myopathy from C-terminal M-band variants, beginning with anterior lower-leg weakness and foot drop.
Recessive titinopathies include early-onset myopathy with fatal cardiomyopathy, congenital core-like myopathy, and Emery-Dreifuss-like phenotypes with contractures.
Heterozygous truncating TTN variants in the A-band are the single commonest genetic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, often without skeletal muscle disease.
Muscle biopsy may show dystrophic changes, rimmed vacuoles or central cores, and calpain-3 can be secondarily reduced, mimicking primary calpainopathy.
Because TTN is enormous, deep intronic and structural variants can be missed, and pathogenicity interpretation is challenging given frequent benign truncations in the population.
Cardiac surveillance is essential in recessive titinopathy and in carriers of A-band truncating variants given the risk of dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia.
reference.pathophysiology: Titin is the largest protein in the human body and forms a continuous filament from the Z-disc to the M-band, acting as a molecular spring that sets the sarcomere's passive tension and resting length, serving as a template for sarcomere assembly and participating in mechanosensing and signalling. Its extreme size and multiple isoforms mean that the functional consequence of a variant depends critically on which domain and which exons are affected and whether those exons are constitutively expressed. M-band variants disrupt the C-terminal kinase region and interaction with calpain-3 and are responsible for dominant tibial muscular dystrophy and, in the homozygous or compound state, more severe limb-girdle and early-onset phenotypes; secondary calpain-3 deficiency explains overlap with calpainopathy on biopsy. Variants affecting the elastic I-band or the structural A-band, and biallelic combinations, produce congenital myopathy, cardiomyopathy and contractural (Emery-Dreifuss-like) phenotypes. In the heart, heterozygous truncating variants clustered in the A-band impair sarcomere integrity under haemodynamic load, producing dilated cardiomyopathy with a propensity to arrhythmia, whereas equivalent truncations in exons not highly expressed in the heart may be clinically silent.
additionalDifferentials: Calpainopathy and other limb-girdle muscular dystrophies
Myofibrillar myopathies including filaminopathy and desminopathy
Other genetic dilated cardiomyopathies (lamin A/C, filamin C)
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive TTN analysis (next-generation sequencing with copy-number and, where possible, deep-intronic assessment) and segregation studies
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry, including calpain-3 immunoblot and assessment for cores/rimmed vacuoles
Muscle MRI to characterise the selective pattern of muscle involvement
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI for dilated cardiomyopathy and fibrosis
ECG and ambulatory rhythm monitoring for arrhythmia and conduction disease
Respiratory function testing in congenital and severe recessive forms
redFlags: Signs of dilated cardiomyopathy or new arrhythmia, particularly with A-band truncating variants
Early-onset severe myopathy with cardiac involvement in infancy
Contractures with cardiac conduction disease suggesting an Emery-Dreifuss-like course
Family history of premature sudden cardiac death or unexplained heart failure
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies enormously by phenotype: dominant tibial muscular dystrophy is slowly progressive with preserved lifespan and ambulation into later life, whereas recessive early-onset forms with cardiomyopathy can be severe or fatal. Cardiac and respiratory involvement are the principal determinants of outcome.
pitfalls: Misattributing secondary calpain-3 reduction to primary calpainopathy and stopping the diagnostic work-up
Overcalling pathogenicity of TTN truncations given frequent benign variants in the general population
Missing deep intronic or structural variants because of incomplete sequencing coverage
Neglecting cardiac screening in recessive disease and in A-band truncation carriers
Assuming a single uniform phenotype rather than recognising strong domain-dependent variability
references: Inherited cardiomyopathy and cardiovascular genetics references
management: Manage dilated cardiomyopathy with guideline-directed heart failure therapy, as there is no disease-specific drug for the underlying titin defect
Treat arrhythmia and conduction disease and offer an implantable defibrillator or pacemaker where indicated for high-risk cardiac phenotypes
Support weakness with physiotherapy, ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, occupational therapy and management of contractures
Monitor respiratory function and provide non-invasive ventilation for respiratory muscle failure, particularly in congenital and severe recessive forms
Undertake cardiac surveillance with echocardiography, cardiac MRI and ambulatory rhythm monitoring, including in relatives
Offer genetic counselling and cascade screening, tailoring advice to the domain and inheritance pattern of the variant
Coordinate care between neuromuscular neurology and cardiology
